A major milestone in space exploration is happening Wednesday morning as NASA's Voyager 1 will reach the distance of one light day from Earth. A light day is a measure of how far light moves in 24 hours. At a speed of 186,000 miles per second, one light day is 16 billion miles. One light day is the farthest away any object made by humanity has ever traveled from Earth. Voyager 1 launched in 1977 with a team that included a University of New Hampshire scientist. News 9 spoke to the late Dr. William Webber in 1989. He said even then, NASA never expected Voyager to last that long. "When we were designing this instrument and planning it in the early 70s, we never dreamed that it would last more than a few years," Webber said. "This instrument's operated for 15 years perfectly. We still get data from it. UnitedHealth’s model combines UnitedHealthcare insurance with Optum’s care delivery and pharmacy businesses, so the bill aims directly at how the company is built. title: Man charged with OUI, manslaughter in wrong-way crash that killed UNH hockey player - WFSB
content:
NORTH HAVEN, Conn. (WFSB) - State police have charged a 31-year-old man with manslaughter and other counts in an Oct. 16 wrong-way crash on Interstate 91 that killed University of New Haven student, 21-year-old Ryan O’Shea. Troopers charged Guillermo Carmona-Lopez after obtaining an arrest warrant, police said. He was arrested Nov. 9 and arraigned from a hospital bed. Troopers responded to I-91 southbound near Exit 9 in North Haven for a report of a wrong-way crash, state police said. A preliminary investigation found O’Shea was driving a Honda Accord south in the left lane. Carmona-Lopez was driving a Chevrolet Silverado north in the southbound lanes and hit the Accord head-on, according to police. The Accord went into the left-center lane, where a Jeep Grand Cherokee hit it, police said. The Accord then went into the right lane and onto the right shoulder, where a GMC Terrain hit it. O’Shea was pronounced dead at the scene. Carmona-Lopez was taken to Yale New Haven Hospital with serious, life-threatening injuries, police said. The other drivers were hospitalized with minor injuries. State police said Carmona-Lopez’s license was suspended. One witness told police that as they neared the Exit 8 off-ramp, he saw headlights coming toward them. The witness said there was a car in the left lane approaching them, according to the account police recorded. Another witness captured the collision on a dash camera. Police said the video shows Carmona-Lopez’s truck drove toward and passed at least 18 vehicles before it struck O’Shea’s car. A trooper at the scene said Carmona-Lopez could not explain what happened and smelled of alcohol. Carmona-Lopez allegedly told police in an interview at the hospital that he drank four beers starting around 8 that night. He also said that once he got on the highway, he did not remember anything after that, according to the account police recorded. The arrest warrant states his blood alcohol level was .22 and .21. The legal limit is .08. He was held on $500,000 bond and had a bedside arraignment at the hospital Nov. 12. At last check, he remained in the custody of the state Department of Correction. U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement said Carmona-Lopez is from Mexico and entered the country illegally. ICE said Border Patrol arrested him in May 2013 after he entered the country illegally. The agency said he was deported, then reentered illegally, which is a felony. ICE said Border Patrol arrested him again and issued a final order of removal. The agency said he got back into the country at an unknown time and place. “Ryan O’Shea was just 21 years old,” said acting ICE Director David J. Venturella. “He was a college student, a hockey player and a young man preparing for a career protecting others. His family should be celebrating his accomplishments and looking forward to his future. Instead, they’re mourning a life tragically cut short. We extend our deepest condolences to Ryan’s family, friends and teammates. His death is a devastating loss, and he deserves to be remembered for the life he lived and the future he was working so hard to build.” O’Shea was a senior at the University of New Haven and an assistant captain on the school’s club hockey team. He was heading home from a game, and he was studying to become a police officer. The university held a remembrance for O’Shea in October and unveiled a plaque with his name on campus. “I think it’s good that they made the arrest, I think it’s necessary and hopefully provide closure to the family and to us on campus here,” said Jack Winzer, a University of New Haven freshman. Police are still investigating the crash. They have not said where they believe Carmona-Lopez got on I-91. He passed a number of cars going the wrong way before the collision. Over time, technology investments could help UnitedHealth manage costs more efficiently and improve care coordination across its insurance and care delivery businesses. UnitedHealthcare serves tens of millions of people across commercial, Medicare and Medicaid plans, making it one of the largest health insurers in the world. Optum serves an even broader population through pharmacy benefit management, care delivery and health data services. This scale gives UnitedHealth significant bargaining power and data insights, but it also attracts regulatory scrutiny. Managements focus on sustainable organic growth reflects a shift from rapid expansion toward improving profitability. title: What is the Climate Action Clinic at UNH and is it right for you? - University of New Hampshire
content: If you're interested in sustainability but aren't sure how to turn it into real-world experience, the Climate Action Clinic at the University of New Hampshire is worth exploring. Open to students of any major, this course puts you to work alongside actual businesses, nonprofits, and communities to help them understand and reduce their carbon footprints. Here's what the Clinic is, what you'll do, and what makes it different from a typical college course. The Climate Action Clinic is a semester-long, two-credit course offered through UNH's Sustainability Institute and Peter T. Paul College of Business and Economics. Students work in small teams to complete a carbon footprint analysis for a real organization, using a professional-grade online platform called SIMAP (Sustainability Indicator Management and Analysis Platform), which is hosted by UNH and used by hundreds of colleges and universities across the country. What is a carbon footprint analysis, and why does it matter? A carbon footprint analysis, also called a greenhouse gas inventory, helps an organization understand how much greenhouse gas pollution it produces, and which activities are driving that pollution. It’s what allows organizations to identify practical, cost-effective ways to reduce their emissions. Carbon accounting is an increasingly marketable professional skill and the Climate Action Clinic is designed to give you a working foundation. Do you need to be a sustainability-related major to participate? No, the Clinic is for all majors. Your team will be from different majors, which strengthens the quality of the analysis and reflects how sustainability work happens in professional settings. For Cole Fuller '24, '26G, who majored in analytical economics, the Clinic connected dots he hadn't expected. "The Clinic was really valuable for me to recognize the connection between my skillset, which was more data/math focused, and my interest in sustainability. As an analytical econ major, I wasn't aware of how much opportunity there would be for me in the field." What’s it like to be in the Clinic and how is it different from a typical course? Students tour a Climate Action Clinic client's facility. You'll apply sustainability concepts to a real problem for a real client, within a real deadline. In the first few weeks, students are introduced to the basics of carbon accounting and are matched with a client organization, which could be a business, nonprofit, or municipality – the range of industries students work with is broad. Teams spend the bulk of the semester working through their client's carbon data, verifying a baseline carbon footprint, and analyzing potential meaningful steps toward emissions reduction goals. The semester wraps up with teams presenting their completed work to clients. A peer mentor, a student who has completed the Clinic at least once, serves as your team leader to help guide and support the whole team. This structure means you're supported throughout the process, even if you come in with no prior experience. It also means there's a path to grow within the Clinic itself. Durga Raja '25, an environmental resource economics and sustainability dual major who is now a consultant at Eversource, started as a student team member in her sophomore year and returned as a peer mentor for five additional semesters. "That experience showed me how sustainability goals can look very different across sectors, while giving me the chance to collaborate with peers, work directly with clients, and make a real impact." Students present data and findings to their Climate Action Clinic client. You’ll develop a working understanding of greenhouse gas accounting standards and carbon neutrality claims, and experience applying those concepts. Beyond the technical skills, you will build consulting experience, practice communicating complex information to non-specialist audiences, and develop team-based project management skills. For some students, the Clinic also clarifies a career direction they hadn't previously considered. Cole Fuller returned to take the Clinic a second time as a peer mentor, went on to complete an AmeriCorps service term focused on residential energy efficiency, earned a master's degree in economics, and is now UNH's Energy Systems Analyst. "The Clinic inspired me to pursue jobs that were more sustainability focused.” If you want hands-on sustainability experience, are curious about carbon or environmental reporting as a career direction, or simply want to contribute to something with real-world impact while earning credit, the Clinic is for you. Because it is open to all majors, it is also a way to explore sustainability work without committing to a full program change. As Cole Fuller's path shows, the skills developed in the Clinic can translate across industries and career directions well beyond what you might initially anticipate. If the Climate Action Clinic sounds like a fit for you, take these next steps: The Climate Action Clinic is offered each spring semester. Check the Clinic website for course pre-registration before spring course registration opens each fall. Explore UNH's sustainability dual major, which can be paired with any primary major and for which the Clinic counts as an elective credit.
